raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department with a cough, dyspnea, fevers, chills, night sweats, and fatigue.
She had never experienced pulmonary symptoms two weeks before presentation when she developed a cough and fever and was prescribed oral levofloxacin for pneumonia by her primary care physician. Completing a 7-day course of antibiotics, with unabating symptoms and worsening dyspnea, she presented to the emergency department for further treatment.
The examination was remarkable for tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 30/min, hypoxemia with an oxygen saturation of 87% in room air, and diffuse bilateral crackles, without jugular venous distension, or lower extremity edema.
Blood test was significant for white blood cell count of 30,000/microL, lactic acid of 5 mEq/L, and a normal metabolic panel. Arterial blood gas revealed a pH of 7.17, PaCO2 of 50 mmHg, HCO3 of 19 mmol/L, PaO2 of 65.3 mmHg, and SaO2 of 87%.
A CT-PE of the chest showed bilateral extensive multifocal infiltrates with significant hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no evidence of pulmonary embolism.
She was intubated for respiratory distress and admitted to the medical intensive care unit, with a tentative diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
A parasite smear and initial blood cultures were negative.
Bronchoscopy done on the day of admission showed mild diffuse erythema without hemorrhage. Given the patient's repeated desaturation during the procedure, transbronchial biopsies were not performed and the procedure terminated early. Lavage was sent for cytology, bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal stain, and culture.
An echocardiogram showed a hyperdynamic left ventricle with an estimated ejection fraction of 70% with severe right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesis. Right ventricular systolic pressure was estimated at 80 mmHg with a tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) of 1.3.
She continued to worsen, with worsening hypoxia and difficulty with mechanical ventilation, ultimately requiring airway pressure release ventilation and inhaled epoprostenol. Bronchoalveolar lavage remained negative, for bacteria, fungi, or Pneumocystis jirovecii sp.
Workup was expanded to include fungal blood cultures, histoplasma and coccidioides serology, and viral respiratory panel. Respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) were negative. Leptospira and pertussis remained negative. Noninfectious workup along autoimmune lines including antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP), and anti-Smith, anti-SCL70, anti-myeloperoxidase (anti-MPO), anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP), and anti-PR3 antibodies all returned negative, with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels on the high end of normal.
She continued to worsen, requiring hemodynamic support with norepinephrine, epinephrine, and vasopressin, with worsening hepatic function and oliguric renal failure.
On the third hospital day, she continued to be febrile. Morning ABG showed a pH of 6.99, PaCO2 of 47.4 mmHg, HCO3 of 10 mmol/L, PaO2 of 88.2 mmHg, SO2 of 83.2%, and lactic acid level of 9 mEq/L; after prompt discussion with the family, the decision was made to start the patient on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support.
However, the patient developed pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest before CRRT could begin, with the eventual demise of the patient.
An autopsy revealed noncaseating granulomata in hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary, splenic, and hepatic parenchyma. Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, and special stains were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic organisms.
Acid-fast bacillary and fungal cultures remained negative. No crystals were seen on polarized microscopy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 41-year-old African American female presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of cough, fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and progressively worsening dyspnea refractory to a 7-day outpatient course of oral levofloxacin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having never experienced prior pulmonary symptoms, the patient developed acute cough and fever 2 weeks prior to admission and completed a 7-day course of oral levofloxacin prescribed by her primary care physician for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. Due to persistent fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath, she presented to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior history of pulmonary disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, severe dyspnea, fevers, chills, night sweats, and fatigue.

objective.physical_examination: Admission examination: Tachypnea with respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, hypoxemia with room-air SpO2 87%, and diffuse bilateral crackles on lung auscultation; no jugular venous distension or lower extremity edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests and arterial blood gas: Marked leukocytosis with WBC 30,000/μL, elevated lactic acid of 5 mEq/L, and normal baseline metabolic panel; admission ABG showed severe mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis with pH 7.17, PaCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mmol/L, PaO2 65.3 mmHg, and SaO2 87% (deteriorating on hospital day 3 to pH 6.99, PaCO2 47.4 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mmol/L, PaO2 88.2 mmHg, SO2 83.2%, and lactate 9 mEq/L alongside acute hepatic and oliguric renal failure). Negative infectious and autoimmune screening: Negative blood and fungal cultures, parasite blood smear, respiratory viral panel (RSV, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus), HIV, EBV, CMV, Histoplasma and Coccidioides serologies, Leptospira, and Bordetella pertussis; negative ANA, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Sm, anti-Scl-70, anti-MPO, anti-RNP, and anti-PR3 antibodies, with high-normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Transthoracic echocardiogram: Hyperdynamic LV (EF 70%) with severe right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesis, RVSP 80 mmHg, and reduced TAPSE (1.3 cm) indicative of acute cor pulmonale / severe pulmonary hypertension.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PE): Extensive bilateral multifocal pulmonary infiltrates and prominent hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without pulmonary embolism. Admission bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Mild diffuse mucosal erythema without hemorrhage (transbronchial biopsies aborted due to desaturation); BAL stains and cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Post-mortem autopsy histopathology: Widespread non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and throughout the pulmonary, splenic, and hepatic parenchyma, with negative Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, fungal, parasitic stains/cultures, and negative polarized microscopy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fulminant, fatal systemic and pulmonary sarcoidosis complicated by severe pulmonary hypertension / acute cor pulmonale (RVSP 80 mmHg), refractory hypoxemic/hypercapnic respiratory failure, and multiorgan shock, definitively diagnosed at autopsy by widespread non-caseating granulomas in the lungs, hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, and spleen after comprehensive exclusion of Pneumocystis jirovecii, mycobacterial, fungal, viral, and autoimmune etiologies. Plan and clinical course: Intubated on admission and managed in the MICU with broad-spectrum antibiotics, airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), inhaled epoprostenol, and triple vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin). On hospital day 3, before planned continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and ECMO could be initiated, she suffered a fatal pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest.
